title: Week 7 · Lesson 19: Neurologic Pathophysiology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 7 — Lesson 19: Neurologic Pathophysiology

FNP-level goal

Recognize neurologic symptoms as time-sensitive physiology. Use vascular territory, neuronal excitability, intracranial pressure, and altered-mental-status frameworks to distinguish outpatient complaints from stroke, seizure emergency, CNS infection, hemorrhage, and delirium requiring immediate escalation.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, and TIA at a first-pass clinical level.
  • Use B.E. F.A.S.T. symptoms and last-known-well time to identify stroke emergencies.
  • Recognize headache red flags and distinguish primary headache patterns from secondary dangerous causes.
  • Explain seizure physiology, postictal states, and seizure-emergency triggers.
  • Approach acute confusion as delirium until proven otherwise.

Part 1 — A focused neurologic safety screen

Sudden focal weakness, facial droop, aphasia, visual loss, severe abrupt headache, syncope, seizure, new confusion, meningismus, fever with neurologic change, or rapidly declining consciousness is not a routine outpatient neurology complaint. Establish onset/last-known-well time, glucose when appropriate, medications/anticoagulants, trauma, infection risk, vascular risks, and baseline function while arranging emergency evaluation.

Part 2 — Stroke: loss of brain perfusion or bleeding

Ischemic stroke occurs when arterial occlusion reduces cerebral perfusion. Without oxygen and glucose, ATP falls, ion pumps fail, excitotoxic injury and edema develop, and neurons die. Hemorrhagic stroke results from bleeding into or around the brain, producing direct tissue injury and increased intracranial pressure. Both are emergencies; clinical symptoms alone cannot reliably distinguish them.

Use B.E. F.A.S.T.: Balance loss, Eye/vision changes, Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Record last-known-well time. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia, atrial fibrillation, prior stroke/TIA, and vascular disease.

Part 3 — TIA is a warning stroke

A TIA causes transient focal neurologic symptoms due to temporary cerebral ischemia. Resolution does not make it safe. Brief unilateral weakness, aphasia, vision loss, or imbalance still requires urgent emergency assessment because early recurrent stroke risk is substantial and imaging/risk evaluation can reveal a true infarct or dangerous cause.

Part 4 — Headache: primary pattern versus secondary cause

Migraine and tension-type headache are common, but diagnosis begins with red flags: sudden thunderclap onset, “worst” or new severe headache, focal deficit, fever/neck stiffness, altered mental status, papilledema, pregnancy/postpartum state, cancer/immunosuppression, anticoagulation, head trauma, or new headache at older age. These require urgent evaluation for hemorrhage, infection, mass effect, vascular pathology, hypertensive emergency, or other secondary causes.

Do not use a prior migraine history to dismiss a new or different dangerous headache pattern.

Part 5 — Seizures and postictal physiology

A seizure reflects abnormal, excessive, synchronous neuronal activity. Causes include epilepsy, acute stroke, infection, head trauma, metabolic disturbance, medication/toxin effects, alcohol withdrawal, or hypoglycemia. A postictal period can cause confusion, fatigue, headache, or focal weakness; it must be distinguished from persistent stroke deficit, ongoing nonconvulsive seizure, or another cause of altered consciousness.

Emergency evaluation is needed for a first seizure, seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, repeated seizures without recovery, breathing difficulty, serious injury, pregnancy, water immersion, or prolonged impaired consciousness.

Part 6 — Delirium: acute brain dysfunction

Delirium is acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition, often due to an underlying medical illness. Infection, hypoxia, stroke, seizures, medications, intoxication/withdrawal, pain, dehydration, kidney/liver disease, electrolyte or glucose disorders, and urinary retention are examples of causes. It is not synonymous with dementia, which is generally chronic and progressive.

Sudden confusion is a medical emergency until a dangerous cause is excluded. Compare to baseline, obtain collateral history, and assess airway/breathing/circulation, glucose, oxygenation, temperature, medications, and focal findings.

Part 7 — Diagnostic reasoning

Neurologic diagnosis uses focused history and examination plus targeted tests. For suspected stroke, rapid brain/vascular imaging and laboratory evaluation occur in emergency pathways. For headache, testing follows red flags and pattern. For seizures and delirium, glucose, electrolytes, medication/toxic exposure, infection, oxygenation, renal/hepatic function, and imaging/EEG may be selected based on context. Do not delay emergency transfer to complete an outpatient workup.

Case 1 — Symptoms resolved

A patient has 15 minutes of unilateral arm weakness and speech difficulty, now resolved. This can be TIA, not “anxiety.” The absence of current deficit does not remove the need for emergency assessment and secondary-prevention evaluation.

Case 2 — New thunderclap headache

A patient reports a sudden, maximal-at-onset severe headache with vomiting and neck pain. This is a secondary-headache red flag requiring emergency evaluation for hemorrhage or another dangerous cause.

Case 3 — Acute confusion

An older adult becomes suddenly inattentive and disoriented over hours. Treat as delirium: evaluate for infection, medication effects, hypoxia, metabolic disease, stroke, and other acute causes rather than labeling it dementia based on age.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Determine time course: sudden versus gradual; last known well; baseline function.
  2. Assess immediate threats: focal deficit, consciousness, airway, breathing, glucose, fever/meningismus, trauma, anticoagulation.
  3. For stroke/TIA, emergency transfer is the decision—not outpatient differentiation of ischemia versus hemorrhage.
  4. For headache, actively screen secondary red flags.
  5. For seizure or confusion, find the precipitating medical cause and escalate when unstable.

High-Yield Summary

Stroke: sudden focal deficit is an emergency; use B.E. F.A.S.T. and last-known-well time.
TIA: transient symptoms still require emergency assessment.
Headache: thunderclap onset, focal deficit, fever/neck stiffness, altered mentation, and new high-risk pattern require urgent workup.
Seizure: abnormal neuronal activity; first, prolonged, recurrent, or complicated seizures need emergency care.
Delirium: acute fluctuating attention/cognition due to medical illness until proven otherwise.
